questions.question: By creating a foreign key constraint, the following are usually considered during design -

options.B: Size of database and growth estimation
options.C: Skill and competency of database administrators

questions.explanation: When defining a foreign key, the designer must specify referential-integrity actions such as ON DELETE CASCADE/SET NULL/RESTRICT and ON UPDATE CASCADE, dictating what happens to child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted or its key changes. (B) database sizing/growth is a capacity-planning concern unrelated to the FK's referential-action semantics. (C) DBA skill level is an organizational/staffing matter, not a schema design decision. (D) deployment architecture (web vs desktop) has no bearing on how a foreign key constraint itself is defined.

questions.question: Which of the following is a kind of stored procedure that is executed as a side-effect of some operations on the data?
questions.explanation: A trigger is a special stored procedure that the database automatically fires in response to a defined data event (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table -- it executes as an automatic side-effect, never called directly by the user. Commit (A) is a transaction-control statement that ends a transaction, not a procedure. A Function (B) is explicitly invoked by name/expression, not fired implicitly as a side-effect. 'Alert' (C) is not a real database object at all, just a plausible-sounding distractor.

questions.question: A data storage system that stores highly structured data and that works with data from one or more systems and sources including historical data is best called —
questions.explanation: A data warehouse is defined precisely this way: a subject-oriented, integrated repository that consolidates highly structured, cleaned data pulled from multiple source systems, retained over time for historical trend analysis and reporting. A Data lake (C) is the near-opposite -- it stores raw, often unstructured or semi-structured data without imposing structure upfront. A Database (D) is a single operational system for current transactional data, not an integration point for multiple historical sources. 'Databank' (A) is an informal, non-technical term not used precisely in DBMS theory.

questions.question: The term given to the minimal number of attributes to define a record is called —
questions.explanation: A candidate key is formally defined as a minimal super key -- the smallest set of attributes that still uniquely identifies each record, with no attribute removable without losing uniqueness. A super key (A) is any attribute set that uniquely identifies a record, but need not be minimal (it may contain redundant extra attributes). A primary key (B) is simply the one candidate key selected by the designer to be the table's main identifier, not the general term for minimality itself. 'Minimal key' (C) is not standard relational-model terminology.

questions.question: Super key in the DBMS is —

options.A: Any set of attributes that can functionally define the record
options.B: Any set of attributes that is a subset of all attribute set
options.C: A single attribute that is unique and can address a record
options.D: A password or encryption key that can unlock any encryption

questions.explanation: A super key is any combination of attributes whose values functionally determine (uniquely identify) every tuple in a relation -- it may include extra, non-essential attributes beyond what is strictly needed. (B) is too vague/circular -- every attribute set is trivially 'a subset of all attributes', so this fails to capture the uniqueness requirement that defines a super key. (C) wrongly restricts super keys to a single attribute, but a super key can be composed of multiple attributes together. (D) confuses the database term 'key' with a cryptographic key, an unrelated security concept.

questions.question: ________ design focusses on the data itself, whereas ________ design focusses more on data type, how it is stored and accessed.
questions.explanation: Only option C uses genuine database-design terminology (physical vs logical design), so it must be the intended answer, but the printed word order is suspect. Conceptually, logical design (ER modelling, normalization, schema) concerns the data itself independent of implementation, while physical design concerns how that data is actually stored on disk - data types, indexes, file organisation, access paths. As printed the blanks read 'Physical...logical' which is backwards from the standard textbook mapping, most likely an OCR/typesetting word-order slip. Options A, B and D substitute unrelated pairs (a diagramming notation, two RDBMS products, two key types) that never describe design phases at all.

questions.question:
Normalization of database usually achieves —
i. Data integrity
ii. Reduced redundancy
iii. Data readability
iv. Data security
questions.explanation: Normalization's textbook benefits are reduced redundancy (ii) and improved data integrity/consistency (i), since eliminating duplicate data removes update/insert/delete anomalies. Data readability (iii) is not a standard normalization goal - more tables and joins can even hurt human readability - and normalization has no bearing on data security (iv), which is enforced separately through access control and encryption. Strictly, the correct set is only 'i and ii', which is not offered as a choice; option C is the closest superset containing both genuine benefits, making it the best available answer, though the question itself is arguably flawed for omitting a clean 'i and ii' option.

questions.question: When decomposed tables are joined, which of the following will preserve non-match tuples only on the left table, but not on the right table?
questions.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns every row from the left table plus matching rows from the right table, filling unmatched right-side columns with NULL - so it keeps left-side rows that have no match on the right (non-match tuples only on the left), which is exactly what the question describes. An inner join drops all non-matching rows from both sides. A right outer join does the mirror image, preserving unmatched rows from the right table instead. A natural join is an inner join performed automatically on identically-named columns, so it also discards non-matches. Hence B is the only join type matching the description.

questions.question: Data about relations such as schema of relation is maintained by the relational database system, it is termed as —
questions.explanation: Metadata is literally defined as 'data about data' - information describing the structure, schema, and properties of the actual data rather than the data values themselves, which is precisely what the question describes. A 'catalog' or 'data dictionary' is the physical repository/table set in which the DBMS stores this metadata, so those terms name the storage mechanism rather than the concept being asked about, making them tempting but slightly off-target distractors. Views are simply virtual tables derived from queries and have nothing to do with storing schema information, so option B can be eliminated immediately.

questions.question: ________ is for altering the database design, whereas ________ is for manipulating the data.
questions.explanation: Data Definition Language (DDL) commands such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP change the database's structural design (tables, schemas, constraints), while Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operate on the data stored within that structure. This exactly matches the two blanks. Option B and C pair unrelated markup/query languages that don't map to 'design vs data' at all (XML and HTML are not database sub-languages in this sense). Option D confuses two kinds of executable database objects (stored procedures and functions), neither of which specifically means 'altering design' or 'manipulating data' as a language category.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a "multi-valued attribute" in an ER model?

options.A: An attribute that uniquely identifies each entity in the entity set.
options.B: An attribute that depends on multiple other attributes.
options.C: An attribute that is inherited from another entity set.
options.D: An attribute that can have multiple values for a single entity instance.

questions.explanation: A multi-valued attribute (drawn as a double-oval in ER diagrams) is one where a single entity instance can legitimately hold more than one value at once - for example, a Person entity's 'PhoneNumbers' attribute. Option A describes a key attribute, not a multi-valued one. Option B describes a derived attribute (computed from others), which is an unrelated ER concept. Option C describes attribute inheritance, relevant to generalization/specialization hierarchies, not multi-valued attributes. Only D correctly captures the defining property: multiplicity of values per single entity occurrence.

questions.question: Which SQL clause ensures that the deletion of a row from a parent table also deletes all corresponding rows in the child table that reference it?
questions.explanation: The full referential-integrity clause used in a foreign-key constraint definition is 'ON DELETE CASCADE', which tells the DBMS to automatically propagate deletions from the parent row to all matching child rows. 'CASCADE' alone (option A) is only the action keyword, not the complete clause, making it a close but technically incomplete distractor. TRIGGER (B) is a separate database object that could be hand-coded to achieve similar behaviour, but it is not the built-in SQL clause the question asks about. 'DELETE CHILD' (C) is not valid SQL syntax at all.

questions.question: In BIS, which of the following is a primary challenge when integrating multiple data sources into a unified database for analysis?

options.A: Ensuring real-time transaction processing across all data sources.
options.B: Resolving data inconsistencies and conflicts from different systems.
options.C: Creating user-friendly reports from the integrated data.
options.D: Reducing the overall size of the combined data warehouse.

questions.explanation: In Business Information Systems (BIS) / data-warehousing contexts, the central difficulty of integration is that source systems use different formats, codes, units, and business rules for the same real-world entity, so reconciling these conflicts (a core part of the ETL 'transform' step) is the recognised primary challenge. Real-time transaction processing (A) is a concern of OLTP systems, not analytical integration. Producing friendly reports (C) is a downstream presentation concern that assumes the data is already clean. Reducing warehouse size (D) is a storage-optimisation nicety, not a fundamental integration challenge.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the Database Administrator (DBA) in a database environment?

options.A: Designing the physical schema of the database
options.C: Managing network traffic between clients and servers

questions.explanation: The DBA's core duties centre on the database itself: designing and tuning the physical schema (storage structures, indexes, partitioning), managing security, backup/recovery, and performance - so option A is squarely within the DBA's job. Writing end-user application code (B) and developing database-driven web applications (D) are the responsibilities of application/software developers, not the DBA. Managing network traffic between clients and servers (C) belongs to network administrators. The distractors all describe adjacent IT roles that are often confused with the DBA role in exam questions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of a derived attribute in logical database design?

options.A: An attribute that serves as a foreign key in a relationship.
options.B: An attribute that is shared across multiple entities in an ER model.
options.C: An attribute that is used to enforce uniqueness in a table.
options.D: An attribute that is calculated from other attributes in the database.

questions.explanation: A derived attribute is one whose value is computed from other stored attributes rather than stored independently - the classic textbook example is 'Age', derived from 'DateOfBirth' and the current date. Option A describes a foreign key, an entirely different relational concept used to enforce referential integrity between tables. Option B misdescribes shared/composite attributes or inheritance, not derivation. Option C describes a candidate/unique key constraint. Only D captures the calculation-from-existing-data property that defines a derived attribute.

questions.question: In relational model terminology, table is considered as:
questions.explanation: In Codd's formal relational model terminology, a table corresponds to a 'relation'; a row of the table is a 'tuple', a column is an 'attribute', and the set of legal values an attribute can take is its 'domain'. 'Range' is not a standard relational-model term at all, making it an easy elimination. Candidates often confuse 'domain' (a single column's value set) with 'relation' (the whole table), which is the trap this question tests.

questions.question: Which of the following locks the item from access of any type?
questions.explanation: An exclusive (write) lock prevents every other transaction from acquiring any lock - shared or exclusive - on the same data item while it is held, blocking all forms of concurrent access (read or write) until release. A shared (read) lock, by contrast, allows multiple transactions to hold it simultaneously for reading. 'Implicit' and 'explicit' describe how a lock is acquired (automatically by the system versus deliberately requested by a program), not what kind of access it blocks, so they do not answer the question.

questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning business rules is true?

options.B: It should not be convertible to computer code

questions.explanation: A business rule is a statement that defines or constrains some aspect of the business (e.g. 'an order must have at least one line item'), and such rules commonly express restrictions that get translated into database constraints or application logic - which is precisely their purpose. Good business rules should be as simple and unambiguous as possible, and they SHOULD be convertible into enforceable code/constraints, so (a) and (b) each state the opposite of best practice, leaving (c) as the only true statement and making (d) incorrect.

questions.question: Data warehouse is:

options.A: The actual discovery phase of a knowledge discovery process
options.B: The stage of selecting the right data for a KDD process
options.C: A subject-oriented integrated time variant non-volatile collection of data in support of management

questions.explanation: This is Bill Inmon's classic definition of a data warehouse: it is subject-oriented (organized around business subjects, not applications), integrated (consolidated from multiple sources into a consistent format), time-variant (holds historical data over time), and non-volatile (loaded and read, not routinely updated/deleted) - all in support of management's decision-making. Options (a) and (b) instead describe steps within the broader Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process, of which data warehousing is a supporting infrastructure, not a synonym.

questions.question: Which of the following state a heterogeneous distributed database?

options.A: The same DBMS is used at each location and data are not distributed across all nodes.
options.B: The same DBMS is used at each location and data are distributed across all nodes.
options.C: A different DBMS is used at each location and data are not distributed across all nodes.
options.D: A different DBMS is used at each location and data are distributed across all nodes.

questions.explanation: A heterogeneous distributed database is defined by two properties together: different sites run different DBMS products/versions (heterogeneity), AND the data itself is actually spread, partitioned or replicated across those distributed nodes (the database is genuinely distributed, not just several independent databases). Options (a)-(c) each drop one of these two required properties - keeping the DBMS the same (a, b), or keeping the data non-distributed (a, c) - so only (d) satisfies both defining criteria.

questions.question:
The following SQL is which type of join:
SELECT CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID, ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID, NAME, ORDER_ID
FROM CUSTOMER_T, ORDER_T
WHERE CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID = ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID
questions.explanation: This is an equi-join: two tables are listed in the FROM clause (old-style join syntax) and linked in the WHERE clause with an equality (=) condition on CUSTOMER_ID. A natural join would automatically match same-named columns and show CUSTOMER_ID only once in the output; here both CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID and ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID are selected separately, confirming it is an explicit equi-join, not a natural join. There is no outer join keyword, so unmatched rows are dropped, and it is not a Cartesian join because a matching condition is present, not a full cross product.

questions.question: Which of the following is a transitive dependency?

options.A: A functional dependency between two or more key attributes.
options.B: A functional dependency between two or more nonkey attributes.
options.C: A relation that is in first normal form.
options.D: A relation that is in second normal form.

questions.explanation: A transitive dependency exists when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (X -> Y -> Z, where Y and Z are both non-key), rather than depending directly on the primary key. Option (A) describes a dependency among key attributes, which is not transitive by definition. Options (C) and (D) describe normal forms, not dependencies themselves -- 3NF is specifically the normal form defined as having no transitive dependencies, which is a related but different concept from the dependency itself.

questions.question: Which type of entity cannot exist in the database unless another type of entity also exists in the database, but does not require that the identifier of that other entity be included as part of its own identifier?
questions.explanation: A weak entity is existence-dependent on another (owner) entity -- it cannot exist if the owner is deleted -- but it can still have its own independent identifier/primary key without borrowing the owner's key. This is distinct from an ID-dependent entity, where the owner's identifier is actually incorporated into the weak entity's own primary key (a stricter sub-case of weak entity). A strong entity has no existence dependency at all, so (B) is wrong, and 'ID-independent entity' is not a standard database term used to describe this dependency.

questions.question: __________ is a special kind of a store procedure that executes in response to certain action on the table like insertion, deletion or updation of data.
questions.explanation: A trigger is a database object that automatically fires in response to specified DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table, exactly as described. A regular stored procedure (A) must be explicitly called by an application or another routine -- it does not fire automatically. A function (C) is called within expressions and returns a value; it is not tied to table-level DML events either. Hence trigger is the only construct matching 'executes in response to' insert/delete/update actions.

questions.question: A system is in a __________ state if there exists a set of transactions such that every transaction in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook definition of deadlock: a cycle of transactions where each one is blocked waiting for a resource (typically a lock) held by another transaction in the same cycle, so none can proceed. 'Waiting' (B) describes a single transaction's state, not the circular, mutual condition described. 'Idle' and 'Ready' describe transactions with no pending work or ready to execute, which is the opposite of being stuck waiting on each other.

questions.question: If a transaction is performed in a database and committed, the changes are taken to the previous state of transaction by:
questions.explanation: Rollback only works on an uncommitted transaction, undoing its changes before COMMIT is issued; once a transaction is committed, ROLLBACK can no longer reverse it. To restore data to a point before a committed transaction, database systems provide Flashback-type technology (e.g. Oracle Flashback Query/Table), which reconstructs an earlier committed state using undo/history data. Since the question specifies the transaction was already committed, Rollback (B) is not applicable, making Flashback the correct mechanism, not 'both' or 'cannot be done'.

questions.question: Which of the join operations do not preserve non matched tuples?
questions.explanation: An inner join returns only rows that have a match in both tables, discarding any unmatched (non-matching) tuples entirely. Left and right outer joins are specifically designed to preserve unmatched rows from one side, padding the missing side with NULLs, so (A) and (B) are the opposite of what is asked. Note that a natural join (D) is technically also a form of equi/inner join and likewise drops unmatched tuples, which makes this question ambiguous between (C) and (D); (C) is chosen as the more general, textbook-standard answer contrasted against the two outer-join options listed.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a set of one or more attributes taken collectively to uniquely identify a record?
questions.explanation: This is the standard definition of a superkey: any set of one or more attributes whose values, taken together, uniquely identify a tuple -- with no requirement that it be minimal. A candidate key (A) is a stricter concept: a superkey with the additional property of minimality (no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness). Since the question's wording omits any minimality requirement, it matches superkey rather than candidate key. A foreign key (D) references another relation's key and is unrelated to uniqueness within its own table; 'sub key' is not a standard relational-model term.

questions.question: A relational database system needs to maintain data about the relations, such as the schema of the relations. This is called:
questions.explanation: DBMSs store descriptive information about the database's own structure (relation schemas, indexes, constraints, etc.) in a dedicated internal store commonly called the system catalog, which the SQL standard exposes via INFORMATION_SCHEMA. 'Metadata' (A) is the correct general category (data about data) but the question asks what this store is specifically 'called', pointing to the more precise term catalog. A transaction log (C) records changes for recovery, not schema information, and while 'data dictionary' (D) is a near-synonym for catalog in many texts, 'catalog' is the term most directly tied to relational-model schema storage.

questions.question: The attribute AGE is calculated from DATE_OF_BIRTH. The attribute AGE is:
questions.explanation: A derived attribute is one whose value can be computed from another stored attribute rather than being stored independently; AGE computed from DATE_OF_BIRTH is the textbook example. It is not multi-valued (an entity has only one age at a time), not composite (it is not made up of sub-parts like a name split into first/last), and 'single valued' merely describes cardinality, not the fact that it is calculated rather than stored -- the question is specifically testing recognition of the 'derived attribute' ER modeling concept.
